question: When a machine takes over a job and keeps its name, what happens to the people in that job, and can today's newest workers move on to new work the way the human computers and programmers did?

issues.note: Hard cut from the warm exterior of the lit windows to a close-up of a desk with a typewriter and a different, darker palette. The subtitle appears only after the cut, so the viewer does not yet know where this is.
The wide classroom shot cuts to a macro desk close-up while the narration is still mid-sentence ('to design the next test'). The shot change does not match the sentence.
The 3D desk scene switches abruptly to a sepia archival photo, a different visual language, with no transition.
The office of desks cuts to a dark archive corridor. The 'second kind of work' caption fades in late, and the corridor has no clear link to the narration about integration.
The archival IBM 704 photo cuts to a 3D hall of many desks. The 'arithmetic went to the machines' narration is illustrated by a full room of people calculating, which seems to show the opposite.
Cutting from the dark office to the programmer close-up while saying 'two job titles' is confusing. The two titles share one image, which separates them poorly.
Narration moves to 'the people just starting out' over an unchanged empty dark office. The picture does not show beginners.
The empty dark office is reused several times for abstract statistics, with nothing new to look at.

The empty dark office again carries long stretches of statistics narration (about 8:20 to 9:20), including R15.1 to R15.2 and R16.1 to R16.4. The same wide shot with little motion is used for too long.
The BLS quote cards are static text for a long stretch (R11.5 to R11.6, R12.1 to R12.3). Little new to look at.
